clinical_safety.purpose: Clinical decision support and retrieval reference; not a substitute for a clinician, local protocols, or emergency services.
clinical_safety.audience_note: Separate lay first aid from clinician-only interventions. Medication lists are not patient-specific prescriptions.
medication_guardrails: Confirm patient identity, age, weight when relevant, allergies, pregnancy status, renal/hepatic function, current medicines, contraindications, and local formulary.
Use current institutional protocols and product labels for exact dosing, preparation, route, monitoring, and contraindications.
Do not delay emergency transport, imaging, reperfusion, CPR, or specialist review to search this knowledge base.
Do not give oral food, drink, or medicines to a person with possible stroke until swallowing safety is assessed.
Medication use in children, pregnancy, older adults, renal impairment, and critical illness requires extra caution and clinician oversight.
clinical_safety.review_status: Draft reference compiled from the sources listed in each file. Must be reviewed and signed off by the institution's clinical lead before clinical deployment.
clinical_safety.jurisdiction_note: Designed as a general reference with India-relevant emergency number context; confirm local emergency numbers, referral pathways, drug availability, and national guidelines.

display_name: Lifestyle disease: diabetes, blood pressure, cholesterol and prevention

diabetes_adult_criteria.notes: Use a standardized laboratory method; conditions affecting red cell turnover or haemoglobin may make HbA1c unreliable.

diabetes_adult_criteria.diabetes_threshold: 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L) or higher after at least 8 hours fasting

diabetes_adult_criteria.test: 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, 2-hour plasma glucose

diabetes_adult_criteria.diabetes_threshold: 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) or higher with classic hyperglycaemia symptoms or hyperglycaemic crisis
diabetes_adult_criteria.notes: Without unequivocal hyperglycaemia, confirm with repeat testing.

diagnosis.confirmation: In the absence of unequivocal hyperglycaemia, diagnosis generally requires two abnormal results from the same or separate tests. Pregnancy uses separate gestational diabetes criteria and local antenatal pathways.
baseline_assessment: History: symptoms, family history, pregnancy history, diet/activity, smoking, alcohol, sleep, medicines including steroids, and cardiovascular/renal history
Vitals: blood pressure, weight/BMI, waist circumference as appropriate
Labs: HbA1c or plasma glucose, lipid profile, creatinine/eGFR, urine albumin-creatinine ratio; liver tests and other tests based on context
Screen for complications: retinal examination, foot/neuropathy exam, kidney assessment, cardiovascular risk, dental and psychosocial needs
urgent_red_flags: Vomiting, abdominal pain, deep rapid breathing, dehydration, fruity breath or confusion: possible diabetic ketoacidosis/hyperglycaemic crisis
Severe hypoglycaemia, seizure, unconsciousness or inability to swallow: emergency response; do not give oral food/drink to an unconscious person
Chest pain, stroke signs, severe breathlessness or acute confusion require emergency evaluation

actions: Agree individualized glucose, blood pressure, lipid, weight and quality-of-life goals.
Review affordability, access, cultural food patterns, health literacy, pregnancy plans, frailty and patient preferences.
Aim for at least 150 minutes/week moderate activity where medically appropriate plus strength work twice weekly.
Prefer minimally processed high-fibre foods, vegetables, pulses, whole grains, nuts and suitable portions; reduce sugary drinks and excess refined carbohydrates.
Support sustainable weight reduction when indicated, smoking cessation, sleep regularity and stress support.
Foot care, vaccines and regular eye/kidney screening according to local guidelines.
For type 2 diabetes, select medicines based on glycaemic efficacy, cardiovascular disease, heart failure, chronic kidney disease, weight goals, hypoglycaemia risk, tolerability, cost and access.

Use GLP-1 receptor agonists and/or SGLT2 inhibitors with demonstrated benefit when indicated for cardiovascular/renal/heart failure risk, even when glucose is near target, according to the current guideline.
Insulin is essential in type 1 diabetes and may be needed in type 2 diabetes with severe symptomatic hyperglycaemia or crisis.
Reassess treatment, adherence, adverse effects and targets regularly.
HbA1c commonly every 3 months when changing therapy or not at goal, and about every 6 months when stable; individualize.
Check renal function and urine albumin at least annually in diabetes, more often if abnormal or medicines require it.
Assess blood pressure, lipids, weight, hypoglycaemia, feet and eye screening at recommended intervals.

medicines.role: Common glucose-lowering option for type 2 diabetes; choice depends on renal function, tolerance and comorbidities.
safety: Gastrointestinal effects are common; slow titration or extended-release may improve tolerance.
Avoid when eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73 m²; review kidney function and acute illness risks.
Consider vitamin B12 monitoring during long-term use.

medicines.role: Important guideline-supported class for selected people with type 2 diabetes, heart failure or chronic kidney disease; agent choice depends on indication and renal function.
safety: Counsel about genital fungal infections, volume depletion and rare euglycaemic ketoacidosis.
Use sick-day/perioperative withholding instructions from current product label and local protocol.
Not a substitute for insulin in type 1 diabetes; ketoacidosis risk must be considered.

medicines.generic_name: GLP-1 receptor agonists (e.g., semaglutide, dulaglutide, liraglutide)
medicines.role: Guideline-supported glucose-lowering and weight-management options; selected agents have cardiovascular benefit and some kidney outcome evidence.
safety: Nausea, vomiting and other gastrointestinal effects can occur; use product-specific titration.
Assess gallbladder/pancreatitis history and other product-specific cautions.
Pregnancy planning and peri-procedural management require clinician review.

medicines.role: High-efficacy glucose and weight-management option for selected adults where approved and appropriate.
medicines.safety: Requires clinician assessment of contraindications, gastrointestinal tolerance, concomitant medicines and local regulatory status.

medicines.role: Required for type 1 diabetes and used for selected type 2 diabetes, pregnancy, severe hyperglycaemia or acute metabolic decompensation.
safety: Dosing is individualized; hypoglycaemia can be life-threatening.
Teach glucose monitoring, injection technique, storage, sick-day rules and hypoglycaemia treatment.
Do not stop basal insulin in type 1 diabetes without urgent specialist advice.

medicines.generic_name: ACE inhibitor or ARB (examples vary by formulary)
medicines.role: May be indicated for hypertension with albuminuria or other specific cardiovascular/renal indications.
medicines.safety: Monitor potassium and renal function; contraindicated in pregnancy. Do not combine ACE inhibitor plus ARB routinely.

medicines.role: Common cardiovascular risk-reduction medicines selected according to age, risk, established ASCVD and local guideline.
medicines.safety: Review interactions, muscle symptoms, liver context and pregnancy considerations; prescribe based on overall risk, not a single cholesterol value alone.

current_medicine_landscape.meaning: Current guideline-emphasized medicine classes, not a verified sales or prescription-volume ranking.
notable_classes: SGLT2 inhibitors for appropriate heart failure/CKD and cardiovascular-risk indications
GLP-1 receptor agonists for selected cardiovascular-risk and weight-management needs
Dual GIP/GLP-1 therapy (tirzepatide) for selected glucose/weight goals
Metformin and insulin remain important depending on clinical context
current_medicine_landscape.selection_principle: ADA Standards of Care 2026 emphasizes person-centred selection and cardiovascular, kidney, weight, hypoglycaemia, tolerability, cost and preference considerations; it does not mean one medicine is best for everyone.
